### Abstract
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR), functioning as a critical ligand-gated ion channel in the nervous system, has recently been implicated to play a role in various non-neuronal tissues. Nonetheless, a comprehensive understanding of its expression patterns, mechanisms of epigenetic control, and functions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) across various malignancies is still lacking. To address this gap, we performed an extensive multi-cancer investigation of CHRNA7 spanning 31 tumor types, leveraging datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance. Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms. The results revealed that CHRNA7 is significantly overexpressed in 11 cancer types, including cholangiocarcinoma, glioblastoma, and lung squamous cell carcinoma, whereas it is underexpressed in 11 other cancer types, including breast cancer (BRCA) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). A noteworthy finding was the inverse correlation between CHRNA7 expression levels and the staging system recommended by the World Health Organization for specific cancers, such as cervical squamous cell carcinoma and thyroid carcinoma. Another interesting finding is that CHRNA7 plays dual prognostic roles [1] as a protective factor in low-grade glioma and rectal adenocarcinoma and [2] as a risk factor in adrenocortical carcinoma, BRCA, and LUAD. Genomic analyses revealed that copy number variations and single nucleotide variations of CHRNA7 are significantly associated with survival outcomes in cancers such as liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) and kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Moreover, these genetic variations exhibit cancer type-specific correlations with tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability, with positive associations in colon aden

### Highlights
• The present study conducted a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis of α7nAChR across 31 cancer types by using datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance.
• Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms.
• The HMSRF algorithm was employed to construct an upstream transcription factor regulatory network of CHRNA7, and its predictive value as a biomarker for chemotherapy and immunotherapy response was validated using the CTR-DB database, providing a foundation for personalized cancer treatment strategies.

### 1. Introduction
Cancer remains one of the most formidable global health threats [ 1 ]. Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy in breast cancer [ [1] , [2] , [3] ], leading to substantial patient outcome improvements, its therapeutic efficacy remains modest in selected metastatic malignancies [ 4 ]. Although numerous reports have explored shared immunological traits to decipher oncogenic mechanisms [ 5 ], focusing on individual malignancies provides only a fragmented view of the complex, multi-layered biology underlying cancer-related genes and pathways. Consequently, adopting a macroscopic ‘pan-cancer’ approach in research holds promise for uncovering the fundamental mechanisms driving oncogenesis across diverse cancers [ [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] ].
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) is one of the most abundant nAChRs in the nervous system. Robust expression is observed in the hippocampus, cerebral cortex, and multiple subcortical limbic structures [ 11 ]. It plays a role in sensory processing information, attention, and reward pathways. Studies have reported a significant reduction in α7nAChR expression in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and schizophrenia [ 12 ]. CHRNA7, encoding the α7nAChR, has been implicated in a spectrum of neurological disorders including schizophrenia, epilepsy, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and sensory processing deficits [ [12] , [13] , [14] ].

### 3. GSEA of the CHRNA7
To gain insights into the role of the CHRNA7 in various types of cancers, we assessed the correlation between the CHRNA7 and other genes with the “psych” package (version 2.4.12) in the R programming environment. Subsequently, we ranked the correlation values in descending order. For enrichment analysis, we utilized the GSEA function within the “clusterProfiler” package. The reference gene set for this analysis was sourced from the Molecular Signatures database (accessible at https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/ ). The significantly enriched signaling pathways were visualized.

### 4.1. Pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7
We first evaluated pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7 in the TCGA database. Our analysis identified elevated CHRNA7 expression in 11 cancer types: cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBC), esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCA), Glioblastoma (GBM), acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), low-grade glioma (LGG), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), pancreatic adenocarcinoma, pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PCPG), skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), and thymoma (THYM). Conversely, diminished expression levels were detected in an additional 11 malignancies: bladder cancer (BLCA), BRCA, cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CESC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), ovarian cancer (OV), prostate cancer (PRAD), renal epithelial dysplasia (READ), testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT), thyroid carcinoma (THCA), and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) ( Fig. 1 A). Additionally, among tumor tissues in the TCGA database, CHRNA7 expression was the highest in PCPG, TCGT, LGG, and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) ( Fig. 1 B). In GTEx normal tissues, CHRNA7 expression peaked in thyroid, testis, esophagus, and ovary. ( Fig. 1 C).

### 4.2. Prognostic significance of the CHRNA7
The analysis of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves indicates that α7nAChR has diagnostic potential as a biomarker for specific cancer types. ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). The ROC value of the CHRNA7 was &gt;0.7 in cancers such as UCEC, BLCA, LUSC, PRAD, sarcoma (SARC), BRCA, ESCA, GBM, COAD, THCA, CHOL, READ, and PCPG, indicating that the CHRNA7 has good diagnostic capability for these cancers ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Subsequently, an evaluation was conducted to determine the prognostic significance of CHRNA7 as a predictive factor for various prognostic outcomes, encompassing overall survival (OS), disease-specific survival (DSS), progression-free interval (PFI), and disease-free interval (DFI), across the 31 cancer types within the TCGA database. The analysis of OS using KM survival curves revealed that CHRNA7 acts as a protective factor for patients with LGG and READ ( Fig. 4 A–D). However, it serves as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, LUAD, STAD, THCA, ( Fig. 4 A and E-K). DSS analysis identified α7nAChR as a protective factor in CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ, and as a risk factor in ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC ( Supplementary Fig. S2F–N ). According to the results of the DFI analysis, the CHRNA7 is a protective factor for patients with COAD, LGG, LUAD, OV, PRAD, and THCA ( Supplementary Fig. S3A–F ) and a risk factor for patients with BLCA, CESC, KIRC, KIRP, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S3G–K ). The PFI analysis identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL and COAD, LGG, OV, and PRAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4A–E ). Conversely, it acts as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, CESC, GBM, KIRC, KIRP, LIHC, LUAD, SARC, SKCM, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4F–P ).

### 4.3. Analyses of genomic alterations in the CHRNA7 and its genomic instability
Genomics strategies are robust approaches to analyze cancer [ 30 ]. In an effort to gauge the potential genomic modifications of the CHRNA7 in specific cancer types, a wide - ranging pan - cancer investigation targeting the copy number variations (CNVs) and single nucleotide variations (SNVs) of the α7nAChR was initiated. CHRNA7 gene amplification was primarily detected in ESCA, SARC, PCPG, and LAML, whereas deep deletions were commonly observed in LUAD, UCS, mesothelioma (MESO), OV, BRCA, BLCA, ACC, KIRC, and LIHC; additionally, A notably elevated frequency of SNVs was observed in cases of UCEC, THYM, STAD, SKCM, and LIHC ( Fig. 5 A and B). Through TIDE analyses relying on the levels of these CNVs, it was found that patients diagnosed with LIHC, KIRC, and BRCA who exhibited elevated levels of CHRNA7 CNVs demonstrated improved survival rates. In contrast, patients with papillary KIRC showed a different survival trend ( Fig. 5 C). Considering the prevalence of these mutations and their potential impact on prognosis and treatment responses, an assessment was made of the relationships between CHRNA7 expression and factors such as TMB, MSI, HRD, aneuploidy, and neoantigens. [ 31 , 32 ]. In COAD, ESCA, and SKCM, CHRNA7 expression showed a significant positive correlation with TMB. ( Fig. 5 D). A comparable positive association between CHRNA7 expression and MSI was observed in COAD, ESCA, GBM, KIRC, OV, READ, and STAD. ( Fig. 5 E). Conversely, CHRNA7 expression correlated negatively with TMB in KIRP ( Fig. 5 D) and with MSI in KICH. ( Fig. 5 E). Regarding HRD, a positive correlation with CHRNA7 expression was found in UCS, THYM, and ACC ( Fig. 5 F). Additionally, a negative correlation between CHRNA7 expression and aneuploidy was detected in COAD ( Fig. 5 G). Tumor-specific neoantigens play a pivotal role as targets for triggering an anti-tumor immune response, and as a result, they are linked to the prognostic outcomes of numerous cancer types. [ 4 ]. ### 4.4. α7nAChR expression is linked to DNA repair, methylation, and cancer cell stemness
The DNA-damage response (DDR) is a complex mechanisms that preserves genomic stability by sensing and resolving sequence or structural anomalies [ 48 ]. Tumor cells can evade therapy by hijacking mismatch repair (MMR [ 34 ] and homologous recombination repair (HRR) [ 35 ] thereby acquiring stem-like self-renewal capacity [ 36 ]. Accordingly, we interrogated the relationships among CHRNA7 expression, MMR-gene profiles, HRR signatures, and stemness. Across cancers, CHRNA7 inversely correlated with multiple MMR genes, most markedly in LUAD, followed by COAD, BRCA, and SKCM. ( Fig. 6 A). Moreover, the CHRNA7 exhibited a positive correlation with the expression of a range of MMR genes in various cancers, including CHOL, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), OV, PCPG, THCA, and LIHC, with the strongest association observed in CHOL ( Fig. 6 A). CHRNA7 expression also showed a significant positive correlation with HRR signatures in ACC, CHOL, MESO, HNSC, TGCT, OV, UCEC, PCPG, UCS and SARC. ( Fig. 6 B). The CHRNA7 also showed a positive correlation with tumor stemness in UCS, THYM, and TGCT ( Fig. 7 C). Collectively, these findings implicate CHRNA7 as a modulator of cancer progression via its capacity to shape DNA-damage repair.
The CHRNA7 is associated with DNA repair, epigenetic modifications, and stemness. (A) Associations between the CHRNA7 and five MMR genes across cancer types are presented in a heatmap. (B) Correlation scatterplots for 10 cancers highlighting correlations between a 30-gene HRR signature and CHRNA7 expression levels. (C) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression levels and stemness are presented with a lollipop chart in which dot sizes are proportional to sample size and dot colors are indicative of p-values. (D) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression and four DNMTs are presented in a heatmap. (E) Pan-cancer differential methylation levels of the CHRNA7 in normal and tumor tissues. ∗p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗p &lt; 0.001. Fig. 7.

### 4.6. Association between the CHRNA7 and pan-cancer ICI and immunotherapy response
CHRNA7 expression positively correlates with both immune and stromal cell abundances in BRCA, LIHC, LUAD, COAD, and READ ( Fig. 8 A). and with ICPs in READ, PRAD, COAD, and LUAD ( Fig. 8 B). CHRNA7 expression was inversely correlated with immune/stromal cell abundances in THCA, SARC, and LGG ( Fig. 8 A) and with immune-checkpoint proteins in ACC, LGG, COAD, and SARC. ( Fig. 8 B). We comprehensively profiled the association between CHRNA7 expression and ICI across 31 cancer by integrating two independent algorithms—ssGSEA and Xcell. Xcell deconvolution further revealed that CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively associated with the infiltration of monocytes, Macrophages, M1-Macrophages, mast cells, DCs, immature DCs and activated DCs in both READ and COAD. Conversely, pronounced inverse correlations with these same myeloid and DC subsets were observed in SARC, THCA and LGG, underscoring a cancer-type-dependent, directionally opposite modulation of the myeloid compartment by CHRNA7 ( Supplementary Fig. S5A ). In BRCA, LUAD, LIHC, READ, COAD, PRAD and DLBC, ssGSEA revealed significant positive correlations between CHRNA7 and the abundance of regulatory T cells (Treg), macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), mast cells, and both central-memory CD8 + and CD4 + T-cell subsets (P &lt; 0.05). Conversely, in LGG, ACC, THCA and SARC, CHRNA7 expression was inversely associated with these same immune populations (all P &lt; 0.05). These convergent yet directionally opposite signatures suggest that CHRNA7 may act as a context-specific immune modulator, potentiating immunosuppressive infiltration in certain malignancies while antagonizing it in others ( Supplementary Fig. S5B ).

### 4.8. Expression analysis of the α7nAChR at the protein level
To identify the expression levels of α7nAChR in normal and cancer tissue cells, we used immunohistochemistry (IHC) and Western Blot (WB) experiments for verification. IHC analysis showed that α7nAChR was expressed at the highest levels in colorectal cancer (CRC) tissues, followed by higher expression levels in macrophages in cancerous tissues, while expression levels in normal tissues were the lowest ( Fig. 9 A–D). Western blotting revealed high α7nAChR expression in colorectal cancer lines HCT116 and HT29, and low expression in LOVO cells and the normal colon line NCM460 ( Fig. 9 E).

### 4.9. The HMSRF algorithm delineated an upstream transcription-factor regulatory network controlling CHRNA7
Transcription factors are proteins that modulate gene expression by specifically binding to cis -regulatory elements within promoter regions, thereby enhancing or repressing RNA-polymerase activity. Here, We hypothesize that upstream TFs dysregulation contributes to the elevated α7nAChR expression observed in COAD. We therefore employed the heuristic multiple-stepwise-regression and information-filtering (HMSRF) algorithm to iteratively reconstruct an upstream multi-layer hierarchical gene regulatory network (ML-hGRN). We applied HMSRF to reconstruct the upstream gene regulatory network and identify key regulators of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A), which consists of 29 genes of α7nAChR, 29 edges, and 8 layers of upstream transcription factors. In this network, MYC (an oncogene) acts as the third layer TF of α7nAChR. Here, MYC promotes the expression of CEBPA, which in turn inhibits TFAP2A. The downregulation of TFAP2A directly induces the upregulation of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A). To evaluate the universality of the associations between CHRNA7 and its putative transcriptional regulators (TFAP2A, CEBPA, and MYC), we analyzed the correlations between CHRNA7 expression and the expression of these transcription factors across multiple cancer types in the TCGA pan-cancer cohort. TFAP2A was found to be positively correlated with CHRNA7 in the majority of cancers, with the strongest correlation in COAD. Correlations for CEBPA and MYC were weaker and more variable. These results indicate that TFAP2A-mediated regulation of CHRNA7 is pan-cancer conserved to some extent, but is particularly pronounced in colorectal cancer, thereby supporting the robustness of the HMSRF model ( Fig. 10 B).
Construction of the upstream transcription factor regulatory network of the HMSRF algorithm based on high expression of α7nAChR. (A) An ML-hGRN of α7nAChR in the discovery set. ### 5. Discussion
Advances in medical technology now enable clinicians to deliver optimal care to cancer patients through surgery, targeted therapy, endocrine therapy, or chemotherapy [ [38] , [39] , [40] ]. However, tumor management alone is not sufficient. Improving the odds of a long-lasting cure through personalized treatment is critical, making the identification of specific tumor targets or characteristics essential [ 41 , 42 ].
Previous studies have examined the expression and function of CHRNA7 in various tumors, such as lung cancer [ 43 ]. However, it remains unelucidated whether the CHRNA7 could function as a prognostic marker in different tumors. This investigation undertook a systematic evaluation of CHRNA7 expression across a spectrum of human tumors. Our findings demonstrate that CHRNA7 is upregulated in 31 cancer types and its expression exhibits significant associations with DNA methylation status, MSI and TMB. Additionally, CHRNA7 overexpression was associated with poor prognosis (PFI, DSS, and OS) of various tumors.
• Kaplan-Meier analysis of overall survival demonstrated that CHRNA7 is a protective factor for LGG and READ, whereas it constitutes a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, STAD, THCA, and LUAD. Univariate Cox regression analysis for Disease-Specific Survival (DSS) identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ. In contrast, it was established as a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC. CHRNA7 exhibits opposite prognostic significance across different cancer types. Integrating GSEA functional enrichment analysis with previous studies, we found that high CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively correlated with the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway in LUAD ( Fig. 8 D). EMT is a critical process through which tumor cells acquire invasive and metastatic capabilities, and its activation typically predicts poor prognosis. Previous studies have demonstrated that CHR

### Abstract
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR), functioning as a critical ligand-gated ion channel in the nervous system, has recently been implicated to play a role in various non-neuronal tissues. Nonetheless, a comprehensive understanding of its expression patterns, mechanisms of epigenetic control, and functions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) across various malignancies is still lacking. To address this gap, we performed an extensive multi-cancer investigation of CHRNA7 spanning 31 tumor types, leveraging datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance. Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms. The results revealed that CHRNA7 is significantly overexpressed in 11 cancer types, including cholangiocarcinoma, glioblastoma, and lung squamous cell carcinoma, whereas it is underexpressed in 11 other cancer types, including breast cancer (BRCA) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). A noteworthy finding was the inverse correlation between CHRNA7 expression levels and the staging system recommended by the World Health Organization for specific cancers, such as cervical squamous cell carcinoma and thyroid carcinoma. Another interesting finding is that CHRNA7 plays dual prognostic roles [1] as a protective factor in low-grade glioma and rectal adenocarcinoma and [2] as a risk factor in adrenocortical carcinoma, BRCA, and LUAD. Genomic analyses revealed that copy number variations and single nucleotide variations of CHRNA7 are significantly associated with survival outcomes in cancers such as liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) and kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Moreover, these genetic variations exhibit cancer type-specific correlations with tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability, with positive associations in colon aden

### Highlights
• The present study conducted a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis of α7nAChR across 31 cancer types by using datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance.
• Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms.
• The HMSRF algorithm was employed to construct an upstream transcription factor regulatory network of CHRNA7, and its predictive value as a biomarker for chemotherapy and immunotherapy response was validated using the CTR-DB database, providing a foundation for personalized cancer treatment strategies.

### 1. Introduction
Cancer remains one of the most formidable global health threats [ 1 ]. Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy in breast cancer [ [1] , [2] , [3] ], leading to substantial patient outcome improvements, its therapeutic efficacy remains modest in selected metastatic malignancies [ 4 ]. Although numerous reports have explored shared immunological traits to decipher oncogenic mechanisms [ 5 ], focusing on individual malignancies provides only a fragmented view of the complex, multi-layered biology underlying cancer-related genes and pathways. Consequently, adopting a macroscopic ‘pan-cancer’ approach in research holds promise for uncovering the fundamental mechanisms driving oncogenesis across diverse cancers [ [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] ].
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) is one of the most abundant nAChRs in the nervous system. Robust expression is observed in the hippocampus, cerebral cortex, and multiple subcortical limbic structures [ 11 ]. It plays a role in sensory processing information, attention, and reward pathways. Studies have reported a significant reduction in α7nAChR expression in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and schizophrenia [ 12 ]. CHRNA7, encoding the α7nAChR, has been implicated in a spectrum of neurological disorders including schizophrenia, epilepsy, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and sensory processing deficits [ [12] , [13] , [14] ].

### 3. GSEA of the CHRNA7
To gain insights into the role of the CHRNA7 in various types of cancers, we assessed the correlation between the CHRNA7 and other genes with the “psych” package (version 2.4.12) in the R programming environment. Subsequently, we ranked the correlation values in descending order. For enrichment analysis, we utilized the GSEA function within the “clusterProfiler” package. The reference gene set for this analysis was sourced from the Molecular Signatures database (accessible at https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/ ). The significantly enriched signaling pathways were visualized.

### 4.1. Pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7
We first evaluated pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7 in the TCGA database. Our analysis identified elevated CHRNA7 expression in 11 cancer types: cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBC), esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCA), Glioblastoma (GBM), acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), low-grade glioma (LGG), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), pancreatic adenocarcinoma, pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PCPG), skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), and thymoma (THYM). Conversely, diminished expression levels were detected in an additional 11 malignancies: bladder cancer (BLCA), BRCA, cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CESC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), ovarian cancer (OV), prostate cancer (PRAD), renal epithelial dysplasia (READ), testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT), thyroid carcinoma (THCA), and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) ( Fig. 1 A). Additionally, among tumor tissues in the TCGA database, CHRNA7 expression was the highest in PCPG, TCGT, LGG, and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) ( Fig. 1 B). In GTEx normal tissues, CHRNA7 expression peaked in thyroid, testis, esophagus, and ovary. ( Fig. 1 C).

(B) CHRNA7 expression in tumor tissues from the TCGA database. The location of the dot represents the mean value of the CHRNA7 expression level. (C) CHRNA7 expression in normal tissues from the GTEx database. We conducted an additional evaluation of CHRNA7 expression across various cancer stages recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). Our findings revealed that for the majority of cancer types, such as CESC, DLBC, KIRP, THCA, and THYM, CHRNA7 expression levels tended 

### 4.2. Prognostic significance of the CHRNA7
The analysis of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves indicates that α7nAChR has diagnostic potential as a biomarker for specific cancer types. ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). The ROC value of the CHRNA7 was &gt;0.7 in cancers such as UCEC, BLCA, LUSC, PRAD, sarcoma (SARC), BRCA, ESCA, GBM, COAD, THCA, CHOL, READ, and PCPG, indicating that the CHRNA7 has good diagnostic capability for these cancers ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Subsequently, an evaluation was conducted to determine the prognostic significance of CHRNA7 as a predictive factor for various prognostic outcomes, encompassing overall survival (OS), disease-specific survival (DSS), progression-free interval (PFI), and disease-free interval (DFI), across the 31 cancer types within the TCGA database. The analysis of OS using KM survival curves revealed that CHRNA7 acts as a protective factor for patients with LGG and READ ( Fig. 4 A–D). However, it serves as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, LUAD, STAD, THCA, ( Fig. 4 A and E-K). DSS analysis identified α7nAChR as a protective factor in CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ, and as a risk factor in ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC ( Supplementary Fig. S2F–N ). According to the results of the DFI analysis, the CHRNA7 is a protective factor for patients with COAD, LGG, LUAD, OV, PRAD, and THCA ( Supplementary Fig. S3A–F ) and a risk factor for patients with BLCA, CESC, KIRC, KIRP, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S3G–K ). The PFI analysis identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL and COAD, LGG, OV, and PRAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4A–E ). Conversely, it acts as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, CESC, GBM, KIRC, KIRP, LIHC, LUAD, SARC, SKCM, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4F–P ).

### 4.3. Analyses of genomic alterations in the CHRNA7 and its genomic instability
Genomics strategies are robust approaches to analyze cancer [ 30 ]. In an effort to gauge the potential genomic modifications of the CHRNA7 in specific cancer types, a wide - ranging pan - cancer investigation targeting the copy number variations (CNVs) and single nucleotide variations (SNVs) of the α7nAChR was initiated. CHRNA7 gene amplification was primarily detected in ESCA, SARC, PCPG, and LAML, whereas deep deletions were commonly observed in LUAD, UCS, mesothelioma (MESO), OV, BRCA, BLCA, ACC, KIRC, and LIHC; additionally, A notably elevated frequency of SNVs was observed in cases of UCEC, THYM, STAD, SKCM, and LIHC ( Fig. 5 A and B). Through TIDE analyses relying on the levels of these CNVs, it was found that patients diagnosed with LIHC, KIRC, and BRCA who exhibited elevated levels of CHRNA7 CNVs demonstrated improved survival rates. In contrast, patients with papillary KIRC showed a different survival trend ( Fig. 5 C). Considering the prevalence of these mutations and their potential impact on prognosis and treatment responses, an assessment was made of the relationships between CHRNA7 expression and factors such as TMB, MSI, HRD, aneuploidy, and neoantigens. [ 31 , 32 ]. In COAD, ESCA, and SKCM, CHRNA7 expression showed a significant positive correlation with TMB. ( Fig. 5 D). A comparable positive association between CHRNA7 expression and MSI was observed in COAD, ESCA, GBM, KIRC, OV, READ, and STAD. ( Fig. 5 E). Conversely, CHRNA7 expression correlated negatively with TMB in KIRP ( Fig. 5 D) and with MSI in KICH. ( Fig. 5 E). Regarding HRD, a positive correlation with CHRNA7 expression was found in UCS, THYM, and ACC ( Fig. 5 F). Additionally, a negative correlation between CHRNA7 expression and aneuploidy was detected in COAD ( Fig. 5 G). Tumor-specific neoantigens play a pivotal role as targets for triggering an anti-tumor immune response, and as a result, they are linked to the prognostic outcomes of numerous cancer types. [ 4 ]. Researchers employe

### 4.4. α7nAChR expression is linked to DNA repair, methylation, and cancer cell stemness
The DNA-damage response (DDR) is a complex mechanisms that preserves genomic stability by sensing and resolving sequence or structural anomalies [ 48 ]. Tumor cells can evade therapy by hijacking mismatch repair (MMR [ 34 ] and homologous recombination repair (HRR) [ 35 ] thereby acquiring stem-like self-renewal capacity [ 36 ]. Accordingly, we interrogated the relationships among CHRNA7 expression, MMR-gene profiles, HRR signatures, and stemness. Across cancers, CHRNA7 inversely correlated with multiple MMR genes, most markedly in LUAD, followed by COAD, BRCA, and SKCM. ( Fig. 6 A). Moreover, the CHRNA7 exhibited a positive correlation with the expression of a range of MMR genes in various cancers, including CHOL, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), OV, PCPG, THCA, and LIHC, with the strongest association observed in CHOL ( Fig. 6 A). CHRNA7 expression also showed a significant positive correlation with HRR signatures in ACC, CHOL, MESO, HNSC, TGCT, OV, UCEC, PCPG, UCS and SARC. ( Fig. 6 B). The CHRNA7 also showed a positive correlation with tumor stemness in UCS, THYM, and TGCT ( Fig. 7 C). Collectively, these findings implicate CHRNA7 as a modulator of cancer progression via its capacity to shape DNA-damage repair.
The CHRNA7 is associated with DNA repair, epigenetic modifications, and stemness. (A) Associations between the CHRNA7 and five MMR genes across cancer types are presented in a heatmap. (B) Correlation scatterplots for 10 cancers highlighting correlations between a 30-gene HRR signature and CHRNA7 expression levels. (C) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression levels and stemness are presented with a lollipop chart in which dot sizes are proportional to sample size and dot colors are indicative of p-values. (D) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression and four DNMTs are presented in a heatmap. (E) Pan-cancer differential methylation levels of the CHRNA7 in normal and tumor tissues. ∗p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗p &lt; 0.001. Fig. 7.

### 4.6. Association between the CHRNA7 and pan-cancer ICI and immunotherapy response
CHRNA7 expression positively correlates with both immune and stromal cell abundances in BRCA, LIHC, LUAD, COAD, and READ ( Fig. 8 A). and with ICPs in READ, PRAD, COAD, and LUAD ( Fig. 8 B). CHRNA7 expression was inversely correlated with immune/stromal cell abundances in THCA, SARC, and LGG ( Fig. 8 A) and with immune-checkpoint proteins in ACC, LGG, COAD, and SARC. ( Fig. 8 B). We comprehensively profiled the association between CHRNA7 expression and ICI across 31 cancer by integrating two independent algorithms—ssGSEA and Xcell. Xcell deconvolution further revealed that CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively associated with the infiltration of monocytes, Macrophages, M1-Macrophages, mast cells, DCs, immature DCs and activated DCs in both READ and COAD. Conversely, pronounced inverse correlations with these same myeloid and DC subsets were observed in SARC, THCA and LGG, underscoring a cancer-type-dependent, directionally opposite modulation of the myeloid compartment by CHRNA7 ( Supplementary Fig. S5A ). In BRCA, LUAD, LIHC, READ, COAD, PRAD and DLBC, ssGSEA revealed significant positive correlations between CHRNA7 and the abundance of regulatory T cells (Treg), macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), mast cells, and both central-memory CD8 + and CD4 + T-cell subsets (P &lt; 0.05). Conversely, in LGG, ACC, THCA and SARC, CHRNA7 expression was inversely associated with these same immune populations (all P &lt; 0.05). These convergent yet directionally opposite signatures suggest that CHRNA7 may act as a context-specific immune modulator, potentiating immunosuppressive infiltration in certain malignancies while antagonizing it in others ( Supplementary Fig. S5B ).

### 4.8. Expression analysis of the α7nAChR at the protein level
To identify the expression levels of α7nAChR in normal and cancer tissue cells, we used immunohistochemistry (IHC) and Western Blot (WB) experiments for verification. IHC analysis showed that α7nAChR was expressed at the highest levels in colorectal cancer (CRC) tissues, followed by higher expression levels in macrophages in cancerous tissues, while expression levels in normal tissues were the lowest ( Fig. 9 A–D). Western blotting revealed high α7nAChR expression in colorectal cancer lines HCT116 and HT29, and low expression in LOVO cells and the normal colon line NCM460 ( Fig. 9 E).

### 4.9. The HMSRF algorithm delineated an upstream transcription-factor regulatory network controlling CHRNA7
Transcription factors are proteins that modulate gene expression by specifically binding to cis -regulatory elements within promoter regions, thereby enhancing or repressing RNA-polymerase activity. Here, We hypothesize that upstream TFs dysregulation contributes to the elevated α7nAChR expression observed in COAD. We therefore employed the heuristic multiple-stepwise-regression and information-filtering (HMSRF) algorithm to iteratively reconstruct an upstream multi-layer hierarchical gene regulatory network (ML-hGRN). We applied HMSRF to reconstruct the upstream gene regulatory network and identify key regulators of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A), which consists of 29 genes of α7nAChR, 29 edges, and 8 layers of upstream transcription factors. In this network, MYC (an oncogene) acts as the third layer TF of α7nAChR. Here, MYC promotes the expression of CEBPA, which in turn inhibits TFAP2A. The downregulation of TFAP2A directly induces the upregulation of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A). To evaluate the universality of the associations between CHRNA7 and its putative transcriptional regulators (TFAP2A, CEBPA, and MYC), we analyzed the correlations between CHRNA7 expression and the expression of these transcription factors across multiple cancer types in the TCGA pan-cancer cohort. TFAP2A was found to be positively correlated with CHRNA7 in the majority of cancers, with the strongest correlation in COAD. Correlations for CEBPA and MYC were weaker and more variable. These results indicate that TFAP2A-mediated regulation of CHRNA7 is pan-cancer conserved to some extent, but is particularly pronounced in colorectal cancer, thereby supporting the robustness of the HMSRF model ( Fig. 10 B).
Construction of the upstream transcription factor regulatory network of the HMSRF algorithm based on high expression of α7nAChR. (A) An ML-hGRN of α7nAChR in the discovery set. ### 5. Discussion
Advances in medical technology now enable clinicians to deliver optimal care to cancer patients through surgery, targeted therapy, endocrine therapy, or chemotherapy [ [38] , [39] , [40] ]. However, tumor management alone is not sufficient. Improving the odds of a long-lasting cure through personalized treatment is critical, making the identification of specific tumor targets or characteristics essential [ 41 , 42 ].
Previous studies have examined the expression and function of CHRNA7 in various tumors, such as lung cancer [ 43 ]. However, it remains unelucidated whether the CHRNA7 could function as a prognostic marker in different tumors. This investigation undertook a systematic evaluation of CHRNA7 expression across a spectrum of human tumors. Our findings demonstrate that CHRNA7 is upregulated in 31 cancer types and its expression exhibits significant associations with DNA methylation status, MSI and TMB. Additionally, CHRNA7 overexpression was associated with poor prognosis (PFI, DSS, and OS) of various tumors.
• Kaplan-Meier analysis of overall survival demonstrated that CHRNA7 is a protective factor for LGG and READ, whereas it constitutes a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, STAD, THCA, and LUAD. Univariate Cox regression analysis for Disease-Specific Survival (DSS) identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ. In contrast, it was established as a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC. CHRNA7 exhibits opposite prognostic significance across different cancer types. Integrating GSEA functional enrichment analysis with previous studies, we found that high CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively correlated with the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway in LUAD ( Fig. 8 D). EMT is a critical process through which tumor cells acquire invasive and metastatic capabilities, and its activation typically predicts poor prognosis. Previous studies have demonstrated that CHR

### Abstract
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR), functioning as a critical ligand-gated ion channel in the nervous system, has recently been implicated to play a role in various non-neuronal tissues. Nonetheless, a comprehensive understanding of its expression patterns, mechanisms of epigenetic control, and functions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) across various malignancies is still lacking. To address this gap, we performed an extensive multi-cancer investigation of CHRNA7 spanning 31 tumor types, leveraging datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance. Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms. The results revealed that CHRNA7 is significantly overexpressed in 11 cancer types, including cholangiocarcinoma, glioblastoma, and lung squamous cell carcinoma, whereas it is underexpressed in 11 other cancer types, including breast cancer (BRCA) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). A noteworthy finding was the inverse correlation between CHRNA7 expression levels and the staging system recommended by the World Health Organization for specific cancers, such as cervical squamous cell carcinoma and thyroid carcinoma. Another interesting finding is that CHRNA7 plays dual prognostic roles [1] as a protective factor in low-grade glioma and rectal adenocarcinoma and [2] as a risk factor in adrenocortical carcinoma, BRCA, and LUAD. Genomic analyses revealed that copy number variations and single nucleotide variations of CHRNA7 are significantly associated with survival outcomes in cancers such as liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) and kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Moreover, these genetic variations exhibit cancer type-specific correlations with tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability, with positive associations in colon aden

### Highlights
• The present study conducted a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis of α7nAChR across 31 cancer types by using datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance.
• Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms.
• The HMSRF algorithm was employed to construct an upstream transcription factor regulatory network of CHRNA7, and its predictive value as a biomarker for chemotherapy and immunotherapy response was validated using the CTR-DB database, providing a foundation for personalized cancer treatment strategies.

### 1. Introduction
Cancer remains one of the most formidable global health threats [ 1 ]. Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy in breast cancer [ [1] , [2] , [3] ], leading to substantial patient outcome improvements, its therapeutic efficacy remains modest in selected metastatic malignancies [ 4 ]. Although numerous reports have explored shared immunological traits to decipher oncogenic mechanisms [ 5 ], focusing on individual malignancies provides only a fragmented view of the complex, multi-layered biology underlying cancer-related genes and pathways. Consequently, adopting a macroscopic ‘pan-cancer’ approach in research holds promise for uncovering the fundamental mechanisms driving oncogenesis across diverse cancers [ [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] ].
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) is one of the most abundant nAChRs in the nervous system. Robust expression is observed in the hippocampus, cerebral cortex, and multiple subcortical limbic structures [ 11 ]. It plays a role in sensory processing information, attention, and reward pathways. Studies have reported a significant reduction in α7nAChR expression in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and schizophrenia [ 12 ]. CHRNA7, encoding the α7nAChR, has been implicated in a spectrum of neurological disorders including schizophrenia, epilepsy, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and sensory processing deficits [ [12] , [13] , [14] ].

### 3. GSEA of the CHRNA7
To gain insights into the role of the CHRNA7 in various types of cancers, we assessed the correlation between the CHRNA7 and other genes with the “psych” package (version 2.4.12) in the R programming environment. Subsequently, we ranked the correlation values in descending order. For enrichment analysis, we utilized the GSEA function within the “clusterProfiler” package. The reference gene set for this analysis was sourced from the Molecular Signatures database (accessible at https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/ ). The significantly enriched signaling pathways were visualized.

### 4.1. Pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7
We first evaluated pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7 in the TCGA database. Our analysis identified elevated CHRNA7 expression in 11 cancer types: cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBC), esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCA), Glioblastoma (GBM), acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), low-grade glioma (LGG), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), pancreatic adenocarcinoma, pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PCPG), skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), and thymoma (THYM). Conversely, diminished expression levels were detected in an additional 11 malignancies: bladder cancer (BLCA), BRCA, cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CESC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), ovarian cancer (OV), prostate cancer (PRAD), renal epithelial dysplasia (READ), testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT), thyroid carcinoma (THCA), and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) ( Fig. 1 A). Additionally, among tumor tissues in the TCGA database, CHRNA7 expression was the highest in PCPG, TCGT, LGG, and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) ( Fig. 1 B). In GTEx normal tissues, CHRNA7 expression peaked in thyroid, testis, esophagus, and ovary. ( Fig. 1 C).

(B) CHRNA7 expression in tumor tissues from the TCGA database. The location of the dot represents the mean value of the CHRNA7 expression level. (C) CHRNA7 expression in normal tissues from the GTEx database. We conducted an additional evaluation of CHRNA7 expression across various cancer stages recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). Our findings revealed that for the majority of cancer types, such as CESC, DLBC, KIRP, THCA, and THYM, CHRNA7 expression levels tended 

### 4.2. Prognostic significance of the CHRNA7
The analysis of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves indicates that α7nAChR has diagnostic potential as a biomarker for specific cancer types. ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). The ROC value of the CHRNA7 was &gt;0.7 in cancers such as UCEC, BLCA, LUSC, PRAD, sarcoma (SARC), BRCA, ESCA, GBM, COAD, THCA, CHOL, READ, and PCPG, indicating that the CHRNA7 has good diagnostic capability for these cancers ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Subsequently, an evaluation was conducted to determine the prognostic significance of CHRNA7 as a predictive factor for various prognostic outcomes, encompassing overall survival (OS), disease-specific survival (DSS), progression-free interval (PFI), and disease-free interval (DFI), across the 31 cancer types within the TCGA database. The analysis of OS using KM survival curves revealed that CHRNA7 acts as a protective factor for patients with LGG and READ ( Fig. 4 A–D). However, it serves as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, LUAD, STAD, THCA, ( Fig. 4 A and E-K). DSS analysis identified α7nAChR as a protective factor in CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ, and as a risk factor in ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC ( Supplementary Fig. S2F–N ). According to the results of the DFI analysis, the CHRNA7 is a protective factor for patients with COAD, LGG, LUAD, OV, PRAD, and THCA ( Supplementary Fig. S3A–F ) and a risk factor for patients with BLCA, CESC, KIRC, KIRP, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S3G–K ). The PFI analysis identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL and COAD, LGG, OV, and PRAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4A–E ). Conversely, it acts as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, CESC, GBM, KIRC, KIRP, LIHC, LUAD, SARC, SKCM, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4F–P ).

### 4.3. Analyses of genomic alterations in the CHRNA7 and its genomic instability
Genomics strategies are robust approaches to analyze cancer [ 30 ]. In an effort to gauge the potential genomic modifications of the CHRNA7 in specific cancer types, a wide - ranging pan - cancer investigation targeting the copy number variations (CNVs) and single nucleotide variations (SNVs) of the α7nAChR was initiated. CHRNA7 gene amplification was primarily detected in ESCA, SARC, PCPG, and LAML, whereas deep deletions were commonly observed in LUAD, UCS, mesothelioma (MESO), OV, BRCA, BLCA, ACC, KIRC, and LIHC; additionally, A notably elevated frequency of SNVs was observed in cases of UCEC, THYM, STAD, SKCM, and LIHC ( Fig. 5 A and B). Through TIDE analyses relying on the levels of these CNVs, it was found that patients diagnosed with LIHC, KIRC, and BRCA who exhibited elevated levels of CHRNA7 CNVs demonstrated improved survival rates. In contrast, patients with papillary KIRC showed a different survival trend ( Fig. 5 C). Considering the prevalence of these mutations and their potential impact on prognosis and treatment responses, an assessment was made of the relationships between CHRNA7 expression and factors such as TMB, MSI, HRD, aneuploidy, and neoantigens. [ 31 , 32 ]. In COAD, ESCA, and SKCM, CHRNA7 expression showed a significant positive correlation with TMB. ( Fig. 5 D). A comparable positive association between CHRNA7 expression and MSI was observed in COAD, ESCA, GBM, KIRC, OV, READ, and STAD. ( Fig. 5 E). Conversely, CHRNA7 expression correlated negatively with TMB in KIRP ( Fig. 5 D) and with MSI in KICH. ( Fig. 5 E). Regarding HRD, a positive correlation with CHRNA7 expression was found in UCS, THYM, and ACC ( Fig. 5 F). Additionally, a negative correlation between CHRNA7 expression and aneuploidy was detected in COAD ( Fig. 5 G). Tumor-specific neoantigens play a pivotal role as targets for triggering an anti-tumor immune response, and as a result, they are linked to the prognostic outcomes of numerous cancer types. [ 4 ]. Researchers employe

### 4.4. α7nAChR expression is linked to DNA repair, methylation, and cancer cell stemness
The DNA-damage response (DDR) is a complex mechanisms that preserves genomic stability by sensing and resolving sequence or structural anomalies [ 48 ]. Tumor cells can evade therapy by hijacking mismatch repair (MMR [ 34 ] and homologous recombination repair (HRR) [ 35 ] thereby acquiring stem-like self-renewal capacity [ 36 ]. Accordingly, we interrogated the relationships among CHRNA7 expression, MMR-gene profiles, HRR signatures, and stemness. Across cancers, CHRNA7 inversely correlated with multiple MMR genes, most markedly in LUAD, followed by COAD, BRCA, and SKCM. ( Fig. 6 A). Moreover, the CHRNA7 exhibited a positive correlation with the expression of a range of MMR genes in various cancers, including CHOL, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), OV, PCPG, THCA, and LIHC, with the strongest association observed in CHOL ( Fig. 6 A). CHRNA7 expression also showed a significant positive correlation with HRR signatures in ACC, CHOL, MESO, HNSC, TGCT, OV, UCEC, PCPG, UCS and SARC. ( Fig. 6 B). The CHRNA7 also showed a positive correlation with tumor stemness in UCS, THYM, and TGCT ( Fig. 7 C). Collectively, these findings implicate CHRNA7 as a modulator of cancer progression via its capacity to shape DNA-damage repair.
The CHRNA7 is associated with DNA repair, epigenetic modifications, and stemness. (A) Associations between the CHRNA7 and five MMR genes across cancer types are presented in a heatmap. (B) Correlation scatterplots for 10 cancers highlighting correlations between a 30-gene HRR signature and CHRNA7 expression levels. (C) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression levels and stemness are presented with a lollipop chart in which dot sizes are proportional to sample size and dot colors are indicative of p-values. (D) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression and four DNMTs are presented in a heatmap. (E) Pan-cancer differential methylation levels of the CHRNA7 in normal and tumor tissues. ∗p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗p &lt; 0.001. Fig. 7.

### 4.6. Association between the CHRNA7 and pan-cancer ICI and immunotherapy response
CHRNA7 expression positively correlates with both immune and stromal cell abundances in BRCA, LIHC, LUAD, COAD, and READ ( Fig. 8 A). and with ICPs in READ, PRAD, COAD, and LUAD ( Fig. 8 B). CHRNA7 expression was inversely correlated with immune/stromal cell abundances in THCA, SARC, and LGG ( Fig. 8 A) and with immune-checkpoint proteins in ACC, LGG, COAD, and SARC. ( Fig. 8 B). We comprehensively profiled the association between CHRNA7 expression and ICI across 31 cancer by integrating two independent algorithms—ssGSEA and Xcell. Xcell deconvolution further revealed that CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively associated with the infiltration of monocytes, Macrophages, M1-Macrophages, mast cells, DCs, immature DCs and activated DCs in both READ and COAD. Conversely, pronounced inverse correlations with these same myeloid and DC subsets were observed in SARC, THCA and LGG, underscoring a cancer-type-dependent, directionally opposite modulation of the myeloid compartment by CHRNA7 ( Supplementary Fig. S5A ). In BRCA, LUAD, LIHC, READ, COAD, PRAD and DLBC, ssGSEA revealed significant positive correlations between CHRNA7 and the abundance of regulatory T cells (Treg), macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), mast cells, and both central-memory CD8 + and CD4 + T-cell subsets (P &lt; 0.05). Conversely, in LGG, ACC, THCA and SARC, CHRNA7 expression was inversely associated with these same immune populations (all P &lt; 0.05). These convergent yet directionally opposite signatures suggest that CHRNA7 may act as a context-specific immune modulator, potentiating immunosuppressive infiltration in certain malignancies while antagonizing it in others ( Supplementary Fig. S5B ).

### 4.8. Expression analysis of the α7nAChR at the protein level
To identify the expression levels of α7nAChR in normal and cancer tissue cells, we used immunohistochemistry (IHC) and Western Blot (WB) experiments for verification. IHC analysis showed that α7nAChR was expressed at the highest levels in colorectal cancer (CRC) tissues, followed by higher expression levels in macrophages in cancerous tissues, while expression levels in normal tissues were the lowest ( Fig. 9 A–D). Western blotting revealed high α7nAChR expression in colorectal cancer lines HCT116 and HT29, and low expression in LOVO cells and the normal colon line NCM460 ( Fig. 9 E).

### 4.9. The HMSRF algorithm delineated an upstream transcription-factor regulatory network controlling CHRNA7
Transcription factors are proteins that modulate gene expression by specifically binding to cis -regulatory elements within promoter regions, thereby enhancing or repressing RNA-polymerase activity. Here, We hypothesize that upstream TFs dysregulation contributes to the elevated α7nAChR expression observed in COAD. We therefore employed the heuristic multiple-stepwise-regression and information-filtering (HMSRF) algorithm to iteratively reconstruct an upstream multi-layer hierarchical gene regulatory network (ML-hGRN). We applied HMSRF to reconstruct the upstream gene regulatory network and identify key regulators of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A), which consists of 29 genes of α7nAChR, 29 edges, and 8 layers of upstream transcription factors. In this network, MYC (an oncogene) acts as the third layer TF of α7nAChR. Here, MYC promotes the expression of CEBPA, which in turn inhibits TFAP2A. The downregulation of TFAP2A directly induces the upregulation of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A). To evaluate the universality of the associations between CHRNA7 and its putative transcriptional regulators (TFAP2A, CEBPA, and MYC), we analyzed the correlations between CHRNA7 expression and the expression of these transcription factors across multiple cancer types in the TCGA pan-cancer cohort. TFAP2A was found to be positively correlated with CHRNA7 in the majority of cancers, with the strongest correlation in COAD. Correlations for CEBPA and MYC were weaker and more variable. These results indicate that TFAP2A-mediated regulation of CHRNA7 is pan-cancer conserved to some extent, but is particularly pronounced in colorectal cancer, thereby supporting the robustness of the HMSRF model ( Fig. 10 B).
Construction of the upstream transcription factor regulatory network of the HMSRF algorithm based on high expression of α7nAChR. (A) An ML-hGRN of α7nAChR in the discovery set. The nodes represent α7nAChR and upstream transcription factors (TFs), the edges represent the regulatory relations (inferred activa

### 5. Discussion
Advances in medical technology now enable clinicians to deliver optimal care to cancer patients through surgery, targeted therapy, endocrine therapy, or chemotherapy [ [38] , [39] , [40] ]. However, tumor management alone is not sufficient. Improving the odds of a long-lasting cure through personalized treatment is critical, making the identification of specific tumor targets or characteristics essential [ 41 , 42 ].
Previous studies have examined the expression and function of CHRNA7 in various tumors, such as lung cancer [ 43 ]. However, it remains unelucidated whether the CHRNA7 could function as a prognostic marker in different tumors. This investigation undertook a systematic evaluation of CHRNA7 expression across a spectrum of human tumors. Our findings demonstrate that CHRNA7 is upregulated in 31 cancer types and its expression exhibits significant associations with DNA methylation status, MSI and TMB. Additionally, CHRNA7 overexpression was associated with poor prognosis (PFI, DSS, and OS) of various tumors.
• Kaplan-Meier analysis of overall survival demonstrated that CHRNA7 is a protective factor for LGG and READ, whereas it constitutes a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, STAD, THCA, and LUAD. Univariate Cox regression analysis for Disease-Specific Survival (DSS) identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ. In contrast, it was established as a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC. CHRNA7 exhibits opposite prognostic significance across different cancer types. Integrating GSEA functional enrichment analysis with previous studies, we found that high CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively correlated with the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway in LUAD ( Fig. 8 D). EMT is a critical process through which tumor cells acquire invasive and metastatic capabilities, and its activation typically predicts poor prognosis. Previous studies have demonstrated that CHR

### Abstract
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR), functioning as a critical ligand-gated ion channel in the nervous system, has recently been implicated to play a role in various non-neuronal tissues. Nonetheless, a comprehensive understanding of its expression patterns, mechanisms of epigenetic control, and functions within the tumor microenvironment (TME) across various malignancies is still lacking. To address this gap, we performed an extensive multi-cancer investigation of CHRNA7 spanning 31 tumor types, leveraging datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance. Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms. The results revealed that CHRNA7 is significantly overexpressed in 11 cancer types, including cholangiocarcinoma, glioblastoma, and lung squamous cell carcinoma, whereas it is underexpressed in 11 other cancer types, including breast cancer (BRCA) and lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). A noteworthy finding was the inverse correlation between CHRNA7 expression levels and the staging system recommended by the World Health Organization for specific cancers, such as cervical squamous cell carcinoma and thyroid carcinoma. Another interesting finding is that CHRNA7 plays dual prognostic roles [1] as a protective factor in low-grade glioma and rectal adenocarcinoma and [2] as a risk factor in adrenocortical carcinoma, BRCA, and LUAD. Genomic analyses revealed that copy number variations and single nucleotide variations of CHRNA7 are significantly associated with survival outcomes in cancers such as liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) and kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Moreover, these genetic variations exhibit cancer type-specific correlations with tumor mutational burden and microsatellite instability, with positive associations in colon aden

### Highlights
• The present study conducted a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis of α7nAChR across 31 cancer types by using datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Genotype-Tissue Expression databases, including its expression patterns, methylation characteristics, genomic instability, and prognostic significance.
• Additionally, the potential immunomodulatory effects of α7nAChR were investigated through integration of multiple algorithms.
• The HMSRF algorithm was employed to construct an upstream transcription factor regulatory network of CHRNA7, and its predictive value as a biomarker for chemotherapy and immunotherapy response was validated using the CTR-DB database, providing a foundation for personalized cancer treatment strategies.

### 1. Introduction
Cancer remains one of the most formidable global health threats [ 1 ]. Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy in breast cancer [ [1] , [2] , [3] ], leading to substantial patient outcome improvements, its therapeutic efficacy remains modest in selected metastatic malignancies [ 4 ]. Although numerous reports have explored shared immunological traits to decipher oncogenic mechanisms [ 5 ], focusing on individual malignancies provides only a fragmented view of the complex, multi-layered biology underlying cancer-related genes and pathways. Consequently, adopting a macroscopic ‘pan-cancer’ approach in research holds promise for uncovering the fundamental mechanisms driving oncogenesis across diverse cancers [ [6] , [7] , [8] , [9] , [10] ].
The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (α7nAChR) is one of the most abundant nAChRs in the nervous system. Robust expression is observed in the hippocampus, cerebral cortex, and multiple subcortical limbic structures [ 11 ]. It plays a role in sensory processing information, attention, and reward pathways. Studies have reported a significant reduction in α7nAChR expression in the brains of patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) and schizophrenia [ 12 ]. CHRNA7, encoding the α7nAChR, has been implicated in a spectrum of neurological disorders including schizophrenia, epilepsy, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and sensory processing deficits [ [12] , [13] , [14] ].

### 3. GSEA of the CHRNA7
To gain insights into the role of the CHRNA7 in various types of cancers, we assessed the correlation between the CHRNA7 and other genes with the “psych” package (version 2.4.12) in the R programming environment. Subsequently, we ranked the correlation values in descending order. For enrichment analysis, we utilized the GSEA function within the “clusterProfiler” package. The reference gene set for this analysis was sourced from the Molecular Signatures database (accessible at https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/ ). The significantly enriched signaling pathways were visualized.

### 4.1. Pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7
We first evaluated pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7 in the TCGA database. Our analysis identified elevated CHRNA7 expression in 11 cancer types: cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBC), esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCA), Glioblastoma (GBM), acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), low-grade glioma (LGG), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), pancreatic adenocarcinoma, pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PCPG), skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM), and thymoma (THYM). Conversely, diminished expression levels were detected in an additional 11 malignancies: bladder cancer (BLCA), BRCA, cervical squamous cell carcinoma (CESC), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), ovarian cancer (OV), prostate cancer (PRAD), renal epithelial dysplasia (READ), testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT), thyroid carcinoma (THCA), and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) ( Fig. 1 A). Additionally, among tumor tissues in the TCGA database, CHRNA7 expression was the highest in PCPG, TCGT, LGG, and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) ( Fig. 1 B). In GTEx normal tissues, CHRNA7 expression peaked in thyroid, testis, esophagus, and ovary. ( Fig. 1 C).
Pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7. (A) Pan-cancer expression of the CHRNA7 between tumor tissues from the TCGA database and normal tissues from the TCGA and GTEx databases. (B) CHRNA7 expression in tumor tissues from the TCGA database. The location of the dot represents the mean value of the CHRNA7 expression level. (C) CHRNA7 expression in normal tissues from the GTEx database. The location of the dot represents the mean value of the CHRNA7 expression level. ∗p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗p &lt; 0.001; and ∗∗∗∗p &lt; 0.0001; ns, not significant. We conducted an additional evaluation of CHRNA7 expression across various cancer stages recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). Our findings revealed that for the majority of cancer types, such as CESC, DLBC, KIRP, THCA, and THYM, CHRNA7 expression levels tended 

### 4.2. Prognostic significance of the CHRNA7
The analysis of Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves indicates that α7nAChR has diagnostic potential as a biomarker for specific cancer types. ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). The ROC value of the CHRNA7 was &gt;0.7 in cancers such as UCEC, BLCA, LUSC, PRAD, sarcoma (SARC), BRCA, ESCA, GBM, COAD, THCA, CHOL, READ, and PCPG, indicating that the CHRNA7 has good diagnostic capability for these cancers ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Subsequently, an evaluation was conducted to determine the prognostic significance of CHRNA7 as a predictive factor for various prognostic outcomes, encompassing overall survival (OS), disease-specific survival (DSS), progression-free interval (PFI), and disease-free interval (DFI), across the 31 cancer types within the TCGA database. The analysis of OS using KM survival curves revealed that CHRNA7 acts as a protective factor for patients with LGG and READ ( Fig. 4 A–D). However, it serves as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, LUAD, STAD, THCA, ( Fig. 4 A and E-K). DSS analysis identified α7nAChR as a protective factor in CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ, and as a risk factor in ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC ( Supplementary Fig. S2F–N ). According to the results of the DFI analysis, the CHRNA7 is a protective factor for patients with COAD, LGG, LUAD, OV, PRAD, and THCA ( Supplementary Fig. S3A–F ) and a risk factor for patients with BLCA, CESC, KIRC, KIRP, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S3G–K ). The PFI analysis identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL and COAD, LGG, OV, and PRAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4A–E ). Conversely, it acts as a risk factor for patients suffering from ACC, BLCA, CESC, GBM, KIRC, KIRP, LIHC, LUAD, SARC, SKCM, and STAD ( Supplementary Fig. S4F–P ).

### 4.3. Analyses of genomic alterations in the CHRNA7 and its genomic instability
Genomics strategies are robust approaches to analyze cancer [ 30 ]. In an effort to gauge the potential genomic modifications of the CHRNA7 in specific cancer types, a wide - ranging pan - cancer investigation targeting the copy number variations (CNVs) and single nucleotide variations (SNVs) of the α7nAChR was initiated. CHRNA7 gene amplification was primarily detected in ESCA, SARC, PCPG, and LAML, whereas deep deletions were commonly observed in LUAD, UCS, mesothelioma (MESO), OV, BRCA, BLCA, ACC, KIRC, and LIHC; additionally, A notably elevated frequency of SNVs was observed in cases of UCEC, THYM, STAD, SKCM, and LIHC ( Fig. 5 A and B). Through TIDE analyses relying on the levels of these CNVs, it was found that patients diagnosed with LIHC, KIRC, and BRCA who exhibited elevated levels of CHRNA7 CNVs demonstrated improved survival rates. In contrast, patients with papillary KIRC showed a different survival trend ( Fig. 5 C). Considering the prevalence of these mutations and their potential impact on prognosis and treatment responses, an assessment was made of the relationships between CHRNA7 expression and factors such as TMB, MSI, HRD, aneuploidy, and neoantigens. [ 31 , 32 ]. In COAD, ESCA, and SKCM, CHRNA7 expression showed a significant positive correlation with TMB. ( Fig. 5 D). A comparable positive association between CHRNA7 expression and MSI was observed in COAD, ESCA, GBM, KIRC, OV, READ, and STAD. ( Fig. 5 E). Conversely, CHRNA7 expression correlated negatively with TMB in KIRP ( Fig. 5 D) and with MSI in KICH. ( Fig. 5 E). Regarding HRD, a positive correlation with CHRNA7 expression was found in UCS, THYM, and ACC ( Fig. 5 F). Additionally, a negative correlation between CHRNA7 expression and aneuploidy was detected in COAD ( Fig. 5 G). Tumor-specific neoantigens play a pivotal role as targets for triggering an anti-tumor immune response, and as a result, they are linked to the prognostic outcomes of numerous cancer types. [ 4 ]. Researchers employe

### 4.4. α7nAChR expression is linked to DNA repair, methylation, and cancer cell stemness
The DNA-damage response (DDR) is a complex mechanisms that preserves genomic stability by sensing and resolving sequence or structural anomalies [ 48 ]. Tumor cells can evade therapy by hijacking mismatch repair (MMR [ 34 ] and homologous recombination repair (HRR) [ 35 ] thereby acquiring stem-like self-renewal capacity [ 36 ]. Accordingly, we interrogated the relationships among CHRNA7 expression, MMR-gene profiles, HRR signatures, and stemness. Across cancers, CHRNA7 inversely correlated with multiple MMR genes, most markedly in LUAD, followed by COAD, BRCA, and SKCM. ( Fig. 6 A). Moreover, the CHRNA7 exhibited a positive correlation with the expression of a range of MMR genes in various cancers, including CHOL, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), OV, PCPG, THCA, and LIHC, with the strongest association observed in CHOL ( Fig. 6 A). CHRNA7 expression also showed a significant positive correlation with HRR signatures in ACC, CHOL, MESO, HNSC, TGCT, OV, UCEC, PCPG, UCS and SARC. ( Fig. 6 B). The CHRNA7 also showed a positive correlation with tumor stemness in UCS, THYM, and TGCT ( Fig. 7 C). Collectively, these findings implicate CHRNA7 as a modulator of cancer progression via its capacity to shape DNA-damage repair.
The CHRNA7 is associated with DNA repair, epigenetic modifications, and stemness. (A) Associations between the CHRNA7 and five MMR genes across cancer types are presented in a heatmap. (B) Correlation scatterplots for 10 cancers highlighting correlations between a 30-gene HRR signature and CHRNA7 expression levels. (C) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression levels and stemness are presented with a lollipop chart in which dot sizes are proportional to sample size and dot colors are indicative of p-values. (D) Correlations between CHRNA7 expression and four DNMTs are presented in a heatmap. (E) Pan-cancer differential methylation levels of the CHRNA7 in normal and tumor tissues. ∗p &lt; 0.05; ∗∗p &lt; 0.01; ∗∗∗p &lt; 0.001. Fig. 7.

### 4.6. Association between the CHRNA7 and pan-cancer ICI and immunotherapy response
CHRNA7 expression positively correlates with both immune and stromal cell abundances in BRCA, LIHC, LUAD, COAD, and READ ( Fig. 8 A). and with ICPs in READ, PRAD, COAD, and LUAD ( Fig. 8 B). CHRNA7 expression was inversely correlated with immune/stromal cell abundances in THCA, SARC, and LGG ( Fig. 8 A) and with immune-checkpoint proteins in ACC, LGG, COAD, and SARC. ( Fig. 8 B). We comprehensively profiled the association between CHRNA7 expression and ICI across 31 cancer by integrating two independent algorithms—ssGSEA and Xcell. Xcell deconvolution further revealed that CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively associated with the infiltration of monocytes, Macrophages, M1-Macrophages, mast cells, DCs, immature DCs and activated DCs in both READ and COAD. Conversely, pronounced inverse correlations with these same myeloid and DC subsets were observed in SARC, THCA and LGG, underscoring a cancer-type-dependent, directionally opposite modulation of the myeloid compartment by CHRNA7 ( Supplementary Fig. S5A ). In BRCA, LUAD, LIHC, READ, COAD, PRAD and DLBC, ssGSEA revealed significant positive correlations between CHRNA7 and the abundance of regulatory T cells (Treg), macrophages, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSC), mast cells, and both central-memory CD8 + and CD4 + T-cell subsets (P &lt; 0.05). Conversely, in LGG, ACC, THCA and SARC, CHRNA7 expression was inversely associated with these same immune populations (all P &lt; 0.05). These convergent yet directionally opposite signatures suggest that CHRNA7 may act as a context-specific immune modulator, potentiating immunosuppressive infiltration in certain malignancies while antagonizing it in others ( Supplementary Fig. S5B ).

### 4.8. Expression analysis of the α7nAChR at the protein level
To identify the expression levels of α7nAChR in normal and cancer tissue cells, we used immunohistochemistry (IHC) and Western Blot (WB) experiments for verification. IHC analysis showed that α7nAChR was expressed at the highest levels in colorectal cancer (CRC) tissues, followed by higher expression levels in macrophages in cancerous tissues, while expression levels in normal tissues were the lowest ( Fig. 9 A–D). Western blotting revealed high α7nAChR expression in colorectal cancer lines HCT116 and HT29, and low expression in LOVO cells and the normal colon line NCM460 ( Fig. 9 E).

### 4.9. The HMSRF algorithm delineated an upstream transcription-factor regulatory network controlling CHRNA7
Transcription factors are proteins that modulate gene expression by specifically binding to cis -regulatory elements within promoter regions, thereby enhancing or repressing RNA-polymerase activity. Here, We hypothesize that upstream TFs dysregulation contributes to the elevated α7nAChR expression observed in COAD. We therefore employed the heuristic multiple-stepwise-regression and information-filtering (HMSRF) algorithm to iteratively reconstruct an upstream multi-layer hierarchical gene regulatory network (ML-hGRN). We applied HMSRF to reconstruct the upstream gene regulatory network and identify key regulators of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A), which consists of 29 genes of α7nAChR, 29 edges, and 8 layers of upstream transcription factors. In this network, MYC (an oncogene) acts as the third layer TF of α7nAChR. Here, MYC promotes the expression of CEBPA, which in turn inhibits TFAP2A. The downregulation of TFAP2A directly induces the upregulation of α7nAChR ( Fig. 10 A). To evaluate the universality of the associations between CHRNA7 and its putative transcriptional regulators (TFAP2A, CEBPA, and MYC), we analyzed the correlations between CHRNA7 expression and the expression of these transcription factors across multiple cancer types in the TCGA pan-cancer cohort. TFAP2A was found to be positively correlated with CHRNA7 in the majority of cancers, with the strongest correlation in COAD. Correlations for CEBPA and MYC were weaker and more variable. These results indicate that TFAP2A-mediated regulation of CHRNA7 is pan-cancer conserved to some extent, but is particularly pronounced in colorectal cancer, thereby supporting the robustness of the HMSRF model ( Fig. 10 B).
Construction of the upstream transcription factor regulatory network of the HMSRF algorithm based on high expression of α7nAChR. (A) An ML-hGRN of α7nAChR in the discovery set. The nodes represent α7nAChR and upstream transcription factors (TFs), the edges represent the regulatory relations (inferred activa

### 5. Discussion
Advances in medical technology now enable clinicians to deliver optimal care to cancer patients through surgery, targeted therapy, endocrine therapy, or chemotherapy [ [38] , [39] , [40] ]. However, tumor management alone is not sufficient. Improving the odds of a long-lasting cure through personalized treatment is critical, making the identification of specific tumor targets or characteristics essential [ 41 , 42 ].
Previous studies have examined the expression and function of CHRNA7 in various tumors, such as lung cancer [ 43 ]. However, it remains unelucidated whether the CHRNA7 could function as a prognostic marker in different tumors. This investigation undertook a systematic evaluation of CHRNA7 expression across a spectrum of human tumors. Our findings demonstrate that CHRNA7 is upregulated in 31 cancer types and its expression exhibits significant associations with DNA methylation status, MSI and TMB. Additionally, CHRNA7 overexpression was associated with poor prognosis (PFI, DSS, and OS) of various tumors.
• Kaplan-Meier analysis of overall survival demonstrated that CHRNA7 is a protective factor for LGG and READ, whereas it constitutes a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, LUSC, STAD, THCA, and LUAD. Univariate Cox regression analysis for Disease-Specific Survival (DSS) identified CHRNA7 as a protective factor in patients with CHOL, DLBC, LGG, LUSC, and READ. In contrast, it was established as a risk factor for ACC, BLCA, BRCA, KIRP, SARC, SKCM, STAD, THCA, and UCEC. CHRNA7 exhibits opposite prognostic significance across different cancer types. Integrating GSEA functional enrichment analysis with previous studies, we found that high CHRNA7 expression is significantly positively correlated with the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathway in LUAD ( Fig. 8 D). EMT is a critical process through which tumor cells acquire invasive and metastatic capabilities, and its activation typically predicts poor prognosis. Previous studies have demonstrated that CHR
